verdict: A solid point-of-sale-cost question squarely in the Commission's remit, with real evidence behind the core claim: Consumer Reports' 12,000-subscriber survey found 55% of extended-warranty buyers never filed a claim and the median net return was a loss, and NCLC's dealer-transaction dataset documents markups averaging 83% on service contracts, 151% on GAP and 325% on window etching, plus a statistically significant Hispanic/non-Hispanic markup gap. The weakest points: the claims span three distinct products (auto service contracts, GAP, appliance warranties) stitched into one proposal, which risks an unfocused story; one claim overstates its own evidence; and the proposal is the third 'point-of-sale product that quietly costs more than it looks' topic from this institution (after heat pumps and buy-now-pay-later), which should discount its claimed novelty.
concerns: Depth/coherence: the 12 claims span auto service contracts, GAP insurance, appliance warranties and telemarketer scams - three largely separate markets with separate evidence bases (https://www.nclc.org data is about add-ons generally, not just service contracts; https://blog.yaleappliance.com is appliances only). A script built from this package risks feeling like three loosely related topics rather than one coherent question; the writer will need to pick a lane (likely auto service contracts, which has by far the deepest evidence) rather than cover all of it.

Claim overstates its source: 'Dealer markups roughly double the actual cost of providing the coverage' implies ~100%. NCLC's actual data (https://filearchive.nclc.org/car_sales/report-auto-add-on.pdf) shows the average service-contract markup was 83% and the combined average across service contracts, GAP and etch was 170% - 'roughly double' is closer to the etch/GAP products than service contracts specifically, and the proposal doesn't say which product it means.

A cited study doesn't support what it's listed to support: the FTC/Kenan-Flagler paper (https://www.ftc.gov/system/files/documents/public_events/966823/leevenkataraman_mightiinterestyouinanextendedwarranty_0.pdf, Lee & Venkataraman 2016) is a regression-discontinuity study of *when* used-car buyers purchase extended warranties relative to base-warranty expiry - it is not about markups, claim rates or value-for-money, and only mentions 'high profit margins' in passing without data. It supports none of the 12 claims directly; it's a mismatch between the study list and the claims it's meant to back.

Novelty is inflated: this is the third 'confident sales pitch vs. what the data says you actually get' story for this institution, following heat-pumps (payback claims) and the already-proposed buy-now-pay-later (point-of-sale financing pitched as free/harmless). The subject and question are genuinely distinct from both, so this doesn't fail on overlap, but a 0.95 novelty score overstates how fresh the format is to this channel.

Two named sources returned access-blocked (403) rather than confirmed or dead: https://www.cartalk.com/extended-warranties/are-extended-car-warranties-worth-it and https://www.consumeraffairs.com/automotive/is-an-extended-car-warranty-worth-it.html. Not necessarily a problem (both are well-known consumer sites, likely just bot-blocked), but they couldn't be verified as making the claims attributed to them.

'Reliable car models rarely need the repairs an extended warranty would cover' and 'Independent warranty providers sell the same coverage for much less than dealers' are softer claims - the first is closer to a general truism than a number any single study pins down, and the second is supported only by an analogous example (a credit union's flat $275 GAP fee vs. dealer averages of $629-655) rather than a direct independent-vs-dealer comparison for service contracts.
